title: JavaScript: promises, the microtask queue and workers
summary: One thread and two queues, Promise.all versus allSettled, bounded concurrency and timeouts with AbortSignal, and worker_threads with SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics.

steps.title: One thread, two queues
body: Node and browsers run your JavaScript on **one thread**, like asyncio. Work waits in two queues:
- the **microtask** queue: promise callbacks (`.then`, the code after an `await`) and `queueMicrotask`. It is emptied completely
after every piece of synchronous code;
- the **macrotask** (task) queue: timers (`setTimeout`), I/O callbacks, `setImmediate`. One is taken per turn of the loop.

steps.prompt: A Node API handler runs a synchronous loop that takes 400 ms to build a report. What happens to the other requests during those 400 ms?
options: They all wait: nothing else runs on the event loop until the loop finishes
They run on other threads in parallel
Node pauses the loop to serve them
Only timers are delayed; HTTP requests still run
steps.explain: Same as a blocking call in asyncio. Move CPU-heavy work to a `worker_threads` Worker (or a separate service), or break it into chunks that yield to the loop.

steps.title: Promise.all fails fast; allSettled waits for everyone
body: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as **one** promise rejects (the others keep running; JavaScript promises cannot be cancelled).
`Promise.allSettled` waits for all and tells you each outcome. `Promise.any` takes the first success; `Promise.race` the first to
settle either way. This card runs both, for real.

code: const ok = (v: string, ms: number) => new Promise<string>(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
const down = (ms: number) => new Promise<string>((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('down')), ms));

pairs: every one fulfils, or it rejects with the first rejection

steps.title: Timeouts, limits and real threads
body: - **Timeouts and cancellation**: pass an `AbortSignal` (`fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) })`, Node 18+ and browsers).
Combine signals with `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(2000)])` (Node 20+). It is .NET's linked token, in JavaScript.
- **Bounded concurrency**: there is no built-in semaphore; teams use a small pool (the `p-limit` package) or start N workers that
pull from a shared array index. `Promise.all(urls.map(fetch))` over 5,000 urls opens 5,000 sockets at once.
- **Real parallelism**: `worker_threads` (Node) and Web Workers (browsers) run JavaScript on other threads, each with its own
heap. They talk by message passing (`postMessage`, data is copied), or share memory through a `SharedArrayBuffer`, where the
races are back, and `Atomics.add`, `Atomics.compareExchange` and `Atomics.wait` play the role of `Interlocked` and `Monitor`.

steps.title: Microtasks can starve the loop too
body: Because the microtask queue is emptied completely before the next macrotask, a promise chain that keeps queuing more microtasks
delays every timer and every I/O callback. Here the timer was due first, but four awaited steps run before it.

steps.prompt: Two Workers increment the same `Int32Array` over a `SharedArrayBuffer` with `counter[0]++`, a million times each. What do you expect?
options: Fewer than two million: `counter[0]++` is read, add, write, and the workers race. Use `Atomics.add(counter, 0, 1)`
Exactly two million: JavaScript is single-threaded
A `TypeError`: shared memory cannot be written
Two million, because Workers take turns automatically
steps.explain: Workers are real threads. Shared memory brings back module 4 in full: lost updates, the need for atomics, and for visibility guarantees.
